title: What is the difference between severity (the technical/business IMPACT of a defect) and priority (how URGENTLY it must be fixed), and why can a defect be low-severity but high-priority (e.g. a company-logo typo on the landing page) or high-severity but low-priority (a crash in a rarely-used admin edge case)?
shortTitle: Severity vs priority, and why they can diverge
keyPoints: Severity is the technical and business impact of a defect: how badly it damages functionality, data, or safety
Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to other work, set by business and scheduling factors
They are independent axes: severity is set by the tester based on the failure, priority is set by the product owner based on context
Low-severity high-priority example: a misspelled company name on the public homepage, cosmetic but brand-damaging
High-severity low-priority example: a crash in a rarely used admin edge case with a manual workaround
Always keep severity and priority as separate fields in the tracker to prevent poor triage decisions

s1_definition.oneliner: Severity measures how badly a defect damages the system, priority measures how urgently it must be fixed, and because impact and urgency are different axes a bug can be low-severity high-priority, like a homepage typo, or high-severity low-priority, like a crash in a rarely used admin corner.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Severity** – The degree of technical and business impact a defect has on the system: how badly it breaks functionality, data, or safety. Usually judged by the tester or by the nature of the bug.
- **Priority** – How urgently the defect must be fixed relative to other work. Judged by the product owner or business based on customer impact, revenue, reputation, and scheduling factors.
- **Independence** – They are independent axes: a defect can be any combination of high or low on each.
- **Low-severity high-priority** – A misspelled company name on the public homepage: cosmetic but brand-damaging, so fix it immediately.
- **High-severity low-priority** – A crash in a rarely used admin edge case with a manual workaround: serious but affects almost nobody, so schedule it later.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, severity is "how much damage does this bug do?" and priority is "how soon must we fix it?" A typo in the bank's name splashed across the public homepage does almost no technical damage, so it is low severity, but it embarrasses the brand in front of every visitor, so the business wants it fixed within the hour, making it high priority. On the other hand, a rare crash deep inside an admin screen that only one back-office clerk ever opens is technically a serious crash, high severity, but because almost nobody hits it and there is a manual workaround, the business is fine fixing it next sprint, making it low priority.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Severity and priority are two independent axes of a defect. Severity is the technical and business impact, how badly the defect breaks functionality, correctness, data, or safety, and it is normally set by the tester based on the nature of the failure. Priority is how urgently the defect must be fixed relative to everything else, and it is normally set by the product owner based on how many users are affected, whether there is a workaround, revenue and compliance impact, reputation, and the release schedule.

Because impact and urgency are different questions, the two can point in opposite directions. The classic low-severity, high-priority example is a misspelled company name on the public landing page: technically nothing is broken so severity is trivial, but every visitor sees an embarrassing brand mistake, so the business wants it fixed within the hour. The mirror image is a crash in a rarely used admin edge case: a crash is technically serious so severity is critical, but if only one internal user ever triggers it and a manual workaround exists, the business is comfortable scheduling it for a later sprint.

At the National Bank of India I always kept the two as separate fields in the tracker, and in bug reports I captured the affected-user count and whether a workaround existed, because those are exactly the facts the product owner needs to set priority sensibly. I remember a release week where a homepage typo in the bank's name, technically trivial, was raised to top priority ahead of a genuinely critical but rarely hit admin crash, and being able to explain calmly why that ordering was correct reassured the stakeholders.

Keeping the axes separate stops two failure modes: polishing cosmetic issues while serious bugs wait, and panicking over a scary-sounding bug that does not actually affect anyone.

Remember one sentence: severity is how badly the bug hurts, priority is how soon you fix it, and they are independent axes that you must track separately.
